title: Amazon S3
summary: Object storage: a metadata service maps bucket/key to placements, data nodes store erasure-coded chunks, and the system delivers eleven nines of durability with strong read-after-write consistency.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: PUT / GET / DELETE / LIST objects in buckets; objects up to 5 TB
Multipart upload; versioning; presigned URLs; lifecycle policies
Strong read-after-write and list consistency (S3 since Dec 2020)
Exabytes of data; millions of requests/s

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: At exabyte scale, replication's 3× storage cost is the dominant expense, so erasure coding is the default for durability.

PUT    /{bucket}/{key}                 body = bytes       -> 200 ETag
GET    /{bucket}/{key}   Range: bytes=…                     -> 200 / 206
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploads                             -> UploadId
PUT    /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber=N&uploadId=…            -> ETag (5 MB–5 GB parts)
POST   /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId=…  (complete)
GET    /{bucket}?list-type=2&prefix=logs/&continuation-token=…

blocks.text: Keys are a flat namespace; `/` is just a character. LIST with a prefix is a range scan on the sorted metadata index.

blocks.caption: Front end streams bytes to storage nodes, then commits metadata

items: **PUT:** front end authenticates, splits the object into chunks, erasure-codes them (e.g. 6 data + 3 parity), writes shards to nodes across 3 AZs.
When enough shards are durable, it commits the metadata record (new version) → 200 OK.
**GET:** look up metadata → read any 6 of the 9 shards in parallel → reconstruct → stream to client.
Erasure coding k data + m parity: survives any m shard losses at (k+m)/k storage; spread shards across AZs and failure domains.
Checksums on every chunk, end to end; background scrubbers re-read data and repair silent corruption.
Repair speed matters as much as redundancy: durability = probability that m+1 failures happen before repair finishes.
Deletes are soft for a period; versioning protects against overwrite mistakes.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Durability is a race between failure and repair. More parity buys time; faster, parallel repair shrinks the window.

items: Metadata is the commit point: an object is visible only once its metadata record is written.
S3 made reads strongly consistent by adding a replicated, consistent witness/cache layer that tracks the latest version per key, so caches never serve stale metadata.
Concurrent PUTs to one key: last writer (by commit order) wins; use versioning or conditional writes (`If-None-Match`) to detect it.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Listing millions of keys under a single hot prefix can overload one metadata partition. Partitions split automatically, but spreading key prefixes still helps request rate.

head: Failure
Impact
Mitigation
rows: Reconstruct from remaining shards; parallel repair across many nodes
Lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads

The SDK signs method + key + expiry with the user's secret (SigV4); the front end verifies the signature, no session needed.
Same metadata, different placement: fewer AZs, colder media, or Glacier tape/deep storage with retrieval delay.
It doesn't natively: copy + delete, which is why flat keys plus prefixes are used.
